A1.justification: Both PDFs describe InfiniBench using the same underlying movie and TV-show sources. Their main text, figures, tables, mathematical content, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, despite substantial revisions.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of eight models in Table 2 and human verification results in Appendix A.

after.justification: v3 reports original evaluations of thirteen models, filtering and modality ablations, and human and automated evaluation-reliability studies.

M1.justification: The benchmark-construction procedure changes substantially. v2 uses TVQA+ character boxes and manual outfit selection; v3 specifies person detection, face matching, and DINOv2 filtering. v3 also adds semantic-similarity screening, metadata/subtitle answerability filters, and event-relative question generation (Section 3.2; Appendix B.1). The five generation prompts are retained.

E1.justification: v3 removes the TVQA-derived local-question skill and expands global-appearance coverage beyond The Big Bang Theory to 850 videos (Figure 3). It adds event-relative grounding questions and metadata-only/subtitles-only evaluation scenarios. The underlying MovieNet and six-TV-show sources remain; temporal questions are renamed chronological understanding.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparison set expands from eight to thirteen models. Gemini 2.0 Flash replaces Gemini 1.5 Flash; Qwen, InternVL, LLaVA-OneVision, LongVU, VideoChat-Flash, and InternLM-XComposer models are added. LLaMA-VID, LWM, MovieChat, and LLaVA-NeXT-Interleave disappear from the leaderboard, although some remain discussed.

E3.justification: v3 introduces explicit 80/10/10 training/validation/test allocation and filtered evaluation sets, and expands human verification from 2.5% to 20%. MCQ scoring changes from GPT-based answer matching to exact option matching; open-ended scoring is specified as GPT-4o-mini on 0–10 instead of GPT-4o on 0–5. GPT-4o's frame budget increases from 250 to 450.

E4.justification: v3 adds modality and filtering ablations, frame-count sensitivity, alternative-judge and human-alignment checks, an 'I don't know' option ablation, duplication analysis, and temporal-certificate analysis. The question-generation success/failure examples are retained. Conversely, v2's four model-response case studies in Figures 17–20 are removed.

E5.justification: v2 reports annotation-correctness percentages without evaluator-agreement analysis. v3 introduces Pearson and Spearman correlations and Krippendorff's alpha across automated judges, plus three human ratings per sample on 10% of the test set and human–judge agreement statistics (Section 4.4). Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty for leaderboard performance.

E6.justification: The leaderboard is extensively replaced and new validation, ablation, and reliability results are added. GPT-4o's headline results change from 49.16% and 3.22/5 in v2 to 47.1% and 6.5/10 in v3; changed tasks, settings, and scoring prevent interpreting this as a performance gain or loss. v3 additionally reports metadata-only accuracy of 36.8% before filtering and 27.4% afterward.

T1.justification: v3 Table 3 introduces a mathematical definition of the combined ranking score: 0.5*accuracy/100 + 0.5*score/10. v2 reports accuracy and open-ended scores separately. This is a limited addition to metric definitions; neither version develops theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace the nine-skill framing with eight grounding/reasoning skills and revise the benchmark size from 108.2K to about 91K questions. The longest-average-duration claim is replaced by emphasis on total video hours and narrative complexity. Reliance on pretrained knowledge and the benefits of multimodal input become central findings.

C2.justification: v3 develops v2's tentative pretrained-knowledge explanation into an explicit leakage interpretation and adds a mechanism explaining why fragmented video frames can interfere with coherent subtitle context. It also discusses evaluator self-enhancement bias and defends diversity within movies and TV shows. Dependence on transcripts remains a stated limitation.

D1.justification: v3 adds detailed annotation and timestamp-verification procedures, transcript sourcing and alignment information, similarity thresholds examined, memory limits, subtitle handling, and model configurations. The scoring prompt changes, while generation prompts remain. Appendix A.1 newly specifies withholding the test set, and Appendix B.3 describes annotations-only distribution.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to LongVideoBench, LVBench, Video-MME, MoVQA, newer video models, and semantic-role grounding research. Appendix C introduces explicit positioning around evolving semantic roles and multimodal narratives. These are substantive additions beyond citation renumbering or bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: v3 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, skill descriptions, and experimental discussion. Skills now precede data collection, four high-level categories become grounding/reasoning groups, and experiments are organized into findings and robustness subsections. Appendices A–G are reorganized into A–C, with retained examples and prompts redistributed.

P2.justification: The overview and pipeline graphics are redesigned, statistics displays are reworked, and the multi-panel leaderboard becomes a unified table with frame budgets and an overall score. v3 adds ablation tables, a duplication plot, and a verification-interface screenshot. Retained examples move, while the old model-response figures disappear.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens benchmark validity through expanded timestamped human verification, removal of identified errors, controls for metadata/subtitle shortcuts, and independent judge validation—important gaps in v2. These gains exceed merely adding models or results. Withholding the test set limits independent reproduction, and inconsistent judge names plus the mixed filtered/unfiltered comparison in Section 4.3.3 weaken reporting precision, but the overall improvement in validation is substantial.
